parts.textTemplate: The handshake is one of the oldest greetings in the world. Historians believe it began (1)___ ancient times as a way (2)___ show that a person was not carrying a weapon. By offering an open hand, two strangers could prove (3)___ they meant no harm to each other. Over the centuries, the gesture spread across many cultures and became (4)___ standard way of greeting someone in business and social situations. Today, a firm handshake is often seen (5)___ a sign of confidence, while a weak one can leave a negative impression. In some countries, however, physical greetings like handshakes are becoming less common, and many people now prefer a simple nod or wave instead. Whether this trend (6)___ continue or the handshake will remain popular for centuries to come is difficult to predict.

parts.title: Part 2 — Multiple Matching
parts.skillNote: To'rtta qisqa matn (A-D) beriladi. Har bir gap qaysi matnga tegishli ekanini aniqlang. Diqqat: bir matn bir necha marta ishlatilishi mumkin.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Amira
texts.text: Amira runs a small graphic design studio from her home in Termiz. She started freelancing five years ago and now works with clients across Central Asia. She says the hardest part of running her own business was learning to manage her time, since nobody was telling her what to do each day. She now uses a strict weekly schedule and never works on Sundays, no matter how much work is waiting.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Sardor
texts.text: Sardor manages a logistics company that delivers goods between Surkhandarya and Tashkent. He took over the business from his father ten years ago and has since doubled the number of trucks. His biggest challenge has been finding reliable drivers, so he now offers extra training and a bonus system to keep good employees from leaving for competitors.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Nilufar
texts.text: Nilufar co-founded an online marketplace for local farmers to sell their produce directly to city customers, cutting out expensive middlemen. In the beginning, many farmers were suspicious of selling online and preferred traditional markets. Nilufar spent months visiting villages in person to explain how the platform worked before farmers started trusting it.

texts.label: D
texts.title: Bekzod
texts.text: Bekzod opened a language center offering English and business courses in his hometown. Demand grew so quickly that within a year he had to move to a bigger building and hire three more teachers. He believes the key to his success has been word-of-mouth recommendations from satisfied students rather than paid advertising.

Who took charge of a business that was already established by a family member?
Who had to convince people in person before they trusted a new service?
Who has grown their business mainly through recommendations rather than advertising?
Who offers rewards to stop employees from moving to rival companies?
Who protects their personal time by refusing to work on a certain day?
Who removes an unnecessary step between producers and buyers?
Who needed larger premises soon after starting the business?

parts.title: Part 3 — Matching Headings
parts.text:
Adapting to Remote Work

15) When offices around the world closed almost overnight, most companies had no formal policy for remote work at all. Managers who had always relied on walking over to a colleague's desk suddenly found themselves unable to gauge how their teams were really doing, and many admitted, in later interviews, that the first few weeks felt closer to guesswork than management.

16) Some companies responded by monitoring employees more closely, installing software that tracked keystrokes or took periodic screenshots. While this approach reassured a handful of nervous executives, employee surveys consistently showed that surveillance tools damaged trust far more than they improved output, often making staff feel like suspects rather than colleagues.

17) A smaller group of companies took the opposite approach, focusing entirely on results rather than hours logged. Managers set clear weekly goals and largely left employees to organize their own schedules. Early data suggested this approach worked well for experienced staff, though newer employees sometimes struggled without the informal guidance office life used to provide.

18) One unexpected challenge was the disappearance of casual, unplanned conversations — the kind that happen in a hallway or over coffee, rather than in a scheduled meeting. Several companies tried to recreate this with virtual "coffee chat" software, with mixed success; some employees found the forced scheduling made spontaneous conversation feel oddly artificial.

19) As remote work continued for months rather than weeks, a new concern emerged: many employees reported working longer hours than they had in the office, unable to draw a clear line between work and home life. Companies that ignored this often saw a rise in resignations several months later, once the initial novelty of working from home had worn off.

20) By the time many offices reopened, a significant number of employees requested to keep working remotely, at least part of the time. Businesses that treated the shift as temporary found themselves negotiating from a weaker position than those that had already begun redesigning their long-term policies around flexibility.

options.text: Blurred boundaries between work and rest

parts.title: Part 4 — Multiple Choice + True/False/No Info
parts.text:
The Unlikely Rise of a Local Bookshop

When Malika opened a small bookshop in Termiz eight years ago, most people in her family thought she was making a mistake. Online retailers had already begun undercutting small bookshops on price, and her own relatives suggested she open a clothing store instead, arguing that books were a dying business in the age of smartphones.

Malika disagreed, but not because she thought people would stop buying from online retailers entirely. Instead, she noticed that many of her friends complained about not knowing what to read next among the millions of titles available online. She decided her shop would sell something online retailers could not easily replicate: personal recommendations from someone who had actually read the books.

For the first two years, the shop barely broke even. Malika spent most evenings reading late into the night so she could speak knowledgeably about as many books as possible. Slowly, word spread that her recommendations were unusually accurate, and customers began returning specifically to ask, "What should I read next?" rather than searching for a specific title.

The shop's turning point came when Malika started a small monthly book club, initially just eight people meeting in the shop after closing hours. Members paid a small fee to join, which covered light refreshments, and Malika chose a different book each month based on the group's evolving tastes. Within eighteen months, the club had grown so large that she had to run two separate sessions to fit everyone in.

Today, book club memberships account for nearly a third of the shop's total income, and Malika has hired two part-time staff to help manage the growing membership. She still personally chooses every book club title herself, insisting that this personal touch is the one thing a large online retailer could never fully copy, no matter how sophisticated their recommendation algorithms become.
